report:
I have sufficient evidence now.

## Report

Your skepticism is well-supported by current evidence. Whole-body vibration (WBV) has **not been shown to reduce fracture risk in people with osteoporosis**, largely because there is almost no direct fracture-outcome data.

The most relevant systematic review/meta-analysis (BMJ Open, 2017) specifically examined WBV's effect on fracture risk in adults ≥50. It found that only **one trial actually reported fracture data**, and that trial showed a non-significant reduction (RR=0.47, 95% CI 0.14–1.57, p=0.22) — meaning the result is compatible with no effect, a benefit, or even harm (bmjopen.bmj.com). The authors concluded WBV *may* reduce fracture risk in generally healthy older adults, but evidence in people with existing chronic disease/osteoporosis was insufficient, and no trial has been powered to detect fracture reduction as a primary endpoint.

Bone mineral density (BMD) studies, often used as a fracture-risk surrogate, show only small, inconsistent gains — a 2011 meta-analysis found modest improvement in hip BMD in postmenopausal women but no significant effect at other sites (link.springer.com), and BMD changes of this magnitude don't reliably translate into fracture reduction.

A 2025 methodological critique published via Cochrane-affiliated researchers explicitly cautions against overstating WBV's fall/fracture prevention benefits, noting quality and certainty issues in the underlying trials (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12577057/).

Patient-facing clinical guidance (Royal Osteoporosis Society, via theros.org.uk) states plainly that research is not clear on whether vibration therapy reduces fracture risk, and most studies involved people without osteoporosis.

**Conclusion:** No high-quality trial has demonstrated that WBV prevents fractures in osteoporosis patients; existing evidence is limited to underpowered studies, surrogate BMD outcomes, and non-significant fracture trends—supporting a "no" or "not proven" answer.
